facts: Psalm 19:1-6 portrays the heavens and firmament as declaring God's glory while day and night pass on knowledge without ordinary speech; the communication is poetic and continuous rather than a literal spoken conversation.
Psalm 19:10-11 evaluates the LORD's judgments as more desirable than fine gold and sweeter than honey, joining moral instruction to images of worth, delight, and warning.

Psalm 19 turns in verses 7-11 from the testimony of creation to a series of names for the LORD's instruction—law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, and judgments—so the poem moves from the ordered heavens to covenant instruction.
In Psalm 19:12-13 the speaker asks to be cleared from hidden faults and restrained from presumptuous sins, distinguishing unknown failure from deliberate, self-asserting transgression.

Psalm 19:14 closes by asking that the speaker's words and meditation be acceptable before the LORD, addressed as the speaker's rock and redeemer; the prayer brings the cosmic and instructional movements into worshiper's speech.
The sun imagery in Psalm 19:4-6 uses two similes—a bridegroom leaving his chamber and a runner completing a course—to emphasize joy, strength, and the sun's comprehensive reach within the poem.
